Exploiting synergies between JWST and cosmic 21-cm observations to
uncover star formation in the early Universe
Jiten Dhandha,1,2★Thomas Gessey-Jones,2,3,6 Harry T. J. Bevins,2,3 Simon Pochinda,2,3 Anastasia Fialkov,1,2
Sandro Tacchella,2,3 Eloy de Lera Acedo,2,3 Saurabh Singh,4 and Rennan Barkana5
1Institute of Astronomy, University of Cambridge, Madingley Road, Cambridge CB30HA, UK
2Kavli Institute for Cosmology, Madingley Road, Cambridge CB30HA, UK

ABSTRACT
In the current era of JWST, we continue to uncover a wealth of information about the Universe deep into the Epoch of Reionization.
In this work, we run a suite of simulations using the code 21cmSPACE to explore the astrophysical properties of galaxies in
the early Universe, and their impact on high-redshift observables. We use multi-wavelength observational data including the
global 21-cm signal and power spectrum limits from SARAS 3 and HERA respectively, present-day diffuse X-ray and radio
backgrounds, and UV luminosity functions (UVLFs) from HST and JWST in the range 𝑧= 6 – 14.5 to derive our constraints.
We constrain a flexible model of halo-mass and redshift dependent star-formation efficiency (SFE), defined as the gas fraction
converted into stars, and find that it is best described by little to no redshift evolution at 𝑧≈6 – 10 and rapid evolution at
𝑧≈10 – 15. We derive Bayesian functional posterior distributions for the SFE across this redshift range, inferring that a halo
of mass 𝑀ℎ= 1010 M⊙has an efficiency of 2 – 3% at 𝑧≲10, 12% at 𝑧= 12 and 26% at 𝑧= 15. We also find, through
synergy between SARAS 3 and UVLFs, that the minimum circular velocity for star-formation in halos is 𝑉𝑐= 16.9+25.7
−9.5 km s−1
or equivalently log10(𝑀crit/ M⊙) = 8.29+1.21
−1.08 at 𝑧= 6. Alongside these star-formation constraints, we find the X-ray and radio
efficiencies of early galaxies to be 𝑓𝑋= 0.5+6.3
−0.3 and 𝑓𝑟≲11.7 respectively, improving upon existing works that do not use
UVLF data. Our results demonstrate the critical role of UVLFs in constraining the early Universe, and its synergies with 21-cm
observations, alongside other multi-wavelength observational datasets.
Key words: cosmology: early Universe – cosmology: dark ages, reionization, first stars – galaxies: star formation – galaxies:
high-redshift
1 INTRODUCTION
The early Universe remains an exciting frontier due to its observational and theoretical prospects. Observations of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) at redshift 𝑧≈1100 (𝑡age ∼0.4 Myr
after the Big Bang) have provided us with a snapshot of the Universe in its infancy, while large-scale spectroscopic surveys like
BOSS (Dawson et al. 2013) and DESI (DESI Collaboration et al.
2024) are mapping the nearby Universe in unprecedented detail. The
epochs intervening these bookends of our cosmic history, however,
remain largely unexplored. Recently, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST; Gardner et al. 2006) has opened a new window into
the distant Universe, with its unprecedented sensitivity and resolution, allowing us to probe some of the earliest galaxies at 𝑧≳10
(𝑡age ≲500 Myr) deep into the Epoch of Reionization (EoR). Prior
to the JWST, the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) had provided us
with a wealth of information on the high-redshift Universe, includ-

been made in literature to resolve this discrepancy, including a topheavy initial mass function (IMF) of early stars (e.g. Inayoshi et al.
2022; Wang et al. 2023; Trinca et al. 2024; Hutter et al. 2024), an

In particular, the 21-cm signal is sensitive to the properties of the

and reionization from stellar/quasar ultraviolet emissions (𝑧≲10,
e.g. Madau et al. 1997; Ciardi & Madau 2003)
Detection of this signal is, however, challenging due to its faintness compared to the bright Galactic foregrounds and instrumental
noise. Current experiments aimed at the detection of the 21-cm signal
typically focus on two summary statistics: the sky-averaged global
signal such as EDGES (Bowman et al. 2018), SARAS (Singh et al.
2022), REACH (de Lera Acedo et al. 2022), MIST (Monsalve et al.
2024), RHINO (Bull et al. 2024), PRIZM (Philip et al. 2019); or
the two-point correlation function of spatial variations (power spectrum) such as MWA (Tingay et al. 2013), LOFAR (van Haarlem et al.
2013), HERA (DeBoer et al. 2017) and others1. Future experiments
will be able to go a step further and make 21-cm tomographic maps
(e.g. SKA, Madau et al. 1997), or probe even deeper into the Dark
Ages from moon-based missions (see, e.g. Fialkov et al. 2024, and
references therein).
In 2018, the EDGES collaboration reported a deeper than expected absorption signal at 𝑧≈17 (Bowman et al. 2018). This
tentative detection spurred a flurry of exciting theoretical works on
early Universe physics. To add to this mystery, measurements of
the diffuse cosmic radio background from ARCADE2 (Fixsen et al.
2011) and LWA1 (Dowell & Taylor 2018) hint at an excess above
the known CMB spectrum and known Galactic/extragalactic sources.
Standard astrophysical mechanisms of galactic emissions (Mirocha
& Furlanetto 2019), either synchrotron emission from Pop III supernovae (Jana et al. 2019) or radio-loud accretion of supermassive
blackholes (e.g. Ewall-Wice et al. 2018, 2020) could provide such
a diffuse contribution. They could also be sourced by exotic agents
like annihilating dark matter (Fraser et al. 2018), super-conducting
cosmic strings (Brandenberger et al. 2019), or primordial blackholes
(Mittal & Kulkarni 2022; Acharya et al. 2022). The 21-cm signal,
by its nature, is sensitive to the radio background; an excess there
would naturally boost the amplitude of the signal (Feng & Holder
2018; Fialkov & Barkana 2019), thus explaining both the EDGES

Recently, Pochinda et al. (2024) conducted the most complete work
to date utilizing multi-wavelength synergies alongside the 21-cm signal to constrain properties of the early Universe. Their work uses the
SARAS 3 non-detection of the 21-cm global signal (Singh et al.
2022), the latest HERA upper limits on the 21-cm power spectrum
(HERA Collaboration et al. 2023), and collated measurements of the
cosmic radio background (CRB; Dowell & Taylor 2018) and cosmic X-ray background (CXB; Hickox & Markevitch 2006; Harrison
et al. 2016). In this work, we extend their analysis by exploring a more
flexible star-formation model, and include the most comprehensive
UVLF measurements from HST and JWST available to date as an
additional observable. In particular, we constrain the star-formation
efficiency of galaxies (SFE), an important quantity widely used in
analytic galaxy formation models (e.g. Sun & Furlanetto 2016; Tacchella et al. 2018; Sipple & Lidz 2024), as well as other astrophysical
parameters. In Section 2, we discuss the theoretical framework, including the enhanced SFE model introduced in ths work, followed
by an introduction of the observational data used in Section 3. We
then describe our methodology for Bayesian inference in Section 4,
and present our results in Section 5. We conclude in Section 6.
2 THEORY OF THE EARLY UNIVERSE

describe the code in this section and refer the reader to the original
 papers for detailed descriptions. The code 21cmSPACE is a
 semi-numerical hydrodynamical code that models the evolution of the
 Universe and galaxy formation using a combination of analytic and
 numerical recipes. The code is designed to produce models that can
 predict the observables from the 21-cm signal and the power spectrum
 of the 21-cm signal. The code 21cmSPACE is a suite of models that
 explore the astrophysical and cosmological parameters that control
 the formation of neutral hydrogen in the IGM. The code is designed to
 be flexible and allow for the exploration of a wide range of parameter
 spaces, including those that control the formation of the IGM through
 the radiation sources, stellar remnants, or other exotic sources.
